379.title: Gargi returns: "two questions, like two arrows" — the imperishable (3.8)
379.hook: the woman who was silenced stands up again, like a warrior stringing a bow, with two questions
379.howItsDone: The akshara passage is studied in Vedanta as one of the Upanishads' great descriptions of Brahman by negation; Gargi's two questions are often retold in Hindu teaching as the moment the debate turns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uddalaka asked about the thread and the inner controller, the one in the earth whose body the earth is. Your line was antaryamin. Did you touch the ground and remember? Day three hundred seventy-nine.

Two days ago, Gargi was told: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. She sat down. Now she stands up again, and this time she speaks to the whole room first. Honored scholars, I'll ask him two questions. If he answers them, none of you will ever beat him. Then she turns to Yajnavalkya. As a warrior's son from Kashi or Videha strings his unstrung bow, takes two sharp arrows in his hand, and rises to fight, so I rise against you with two questions. Answer them.
screen: `SHE STANDS UP AGAIN.` → `A WARRIOR STRINGING HIS BOW.` → `TWO QUESTIONS, LIKE TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First arrow. What is above the sky and below the earth and between the two, what people call past, present and future: on what is that woven? On space, Gargi. She bows. Honor to you, Yajnavalkya, for that answer. Get ready for the second. Second arrow. And on what is space woven? This time he doesn't stop her. He answers. That, Gargi, is what the knowers of Brahman call the imperishable, the akshara. It is neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long. Without shadow, without darkness. Without wind, without space. Without taste or smell, without eye or ear, without voice or mind, without breath or mouth, without measure, without inside or outside. It eats nothing, and nothing eats it. Then he says what it does. At the command of this imperishable, Gargi, the sun and moon are held apart. Earth and sky are held apart. Hours, days, months and years are held apart. Rivers run east from the snowy mountains, and others west. And whoever performs rites and austerities for thousands of years without knowing this, it comes to an end. Last time, Gargi asked what holds the worlds of Brahman, as if it were one more thing. This time the answer isn't a thing. It's described almost entirely by what it isn't: neither coarse nor fine. And Gargi turns to the room. Count yourselves lucky if you get away by bowing to him. None of you will beat him. And she falls silent, on her own terms.
screen: `FIRST ARROW: WOVEN ON SPACE.` · `SECOND ARROW: ON WHAT IS SPACE WOVEN?` · `THE IMPERISHABLE: ONLY WHAT IT ISN'T.` · `BOW TO HIM, AND GO HOME.` · then, large: `NEITHER COARSE NOR FINE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with what isn't anything. Sit, and breathe. Let each thing you notice be named and set down. A sound: not that. A sensation in the knee: not that. A thought: not that. Not coarse, like the chair. Not fine, like the thought. Keep setting things down, gently, without hurry. Don't look for what's left. Just rest in the room the setting-down makes. The bell holds the time.
Akshara. The imperishable, what doesn't wear away. The same word means a syllable or a letter, and in Gargi's question, it's what even space is woven on.
Your line: neither coarse nor fine. Today, ask one question you were once told not to ask, kindly, and in the right room. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gargi was put in her place.
what it means: she came back, asked better, and drew out the book's great description of the imperishable.

380.title: Vidagdha Shakalya: how many gods? 3,306 → 33 → 6 → 3 → 2 → 1½ → 1 (3.9)
380.hook: the last challenger asks how many gods there are, and keeps asking until the number counts down to one
380.howItsDone: Hindu traditions hold many forms of the divine together with the conviction that the divine is one; ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti from the Rig Veda is among the most quoted lines for that idea, and the thirty-three gods are named in Vedic ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi came back with two arrows, and drew out the imperishable: neither coarse nor fine, without inside or outside. Did you ask a question you'd been told not to? Day three hundred eighty.

People sometimes say Hindus have three hundred thirty million gods. Here's a much older count, and it's a countdown. The last challenger, Vidagdha Shakalya, asks Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, he answers. Yes, says Shakalya. But how many gods are there, really? Thirty-three. Yes, but how many really? Six. Really? Three. Really? Two. Really? One and a half. And how many gods are there, really? One.

Then Shakalya makes him explain each number. The three thousand and more, Yajnavalkya says, are only their powers. There are really thirty-three: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Adityas, and Indra and Prajapati. The Vasus are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, sun, sky, moon and stars: everything dwells in them. The Rudras are the ten breaths in a person, and the self: when they leave the body, they make people weep. The Adityas are the twelve months, carrying everything along. Indra is the thunder; Prajapati is the sacrifice. The six are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, the sun and the sky. The three are the three worlds. The two are food and breath. The one and a half? The wind that blows, because everything grows in it. It's a pun in Sanskrit; it doesn't translate. And the one? Breath. It is Brahman. They call it That. Notice what didn't happen. Nobody threw away the thirty-three. The countdown doesn't say the many gods were a mistake. It says they open, like a fan folding shut, onto one. A much older verse in the Rig Veda says it in four words: ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. Hindus live this in different ways. Many worship one form of God as supreme, and see the others as that God's forms or helpers. Some honor many deities, each in its place. Advaita teachers hear in the count one reality appearing as many. This passage gives all of them room. The count is real all the way down.
screen: `3,306: ONLY THEIR POWERS.` · `33: VASUS, RUDRAS, ADITYAS, TWO MORE.` · `FOOD AND BREATH; THE WIND; THEN BREATH.` · `EKAM SAD VIPRA BAHUDHA VADANTI.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes counting down. Sit, and breathe. Start wide: notice everything you can hear and feel at once, the many. Then narrow: just three things. Then two: the air coming in, the body receiving it. Then one and a half: the breath, moving. Then one: just breath. Stay there. When the many come back, and they will, count down again, gently. The bell holds the time.
Ekam. One. In the countdown, where three thousand three hundred and six gods fold down to: breath, Brahman, That.
Your line: one. Today, when you see a shrine, a picture, or any sign of someone's faith, remember: truth is one, and the wise speak of it in many ways. Day three hundred eighty.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hindus believe in millions of gods.
what it means: in this count, the many gods are real, and they fold down, step by step, into one.
what a scholar hears: 3.9.1–9's count of 3,306 comes from a ritual formula; the one and a half (adhyardha) is a pun on the wind in which all grows (adhyārdhnot).

381.title: Shakalya's head falls off (3.9)
381.hook: the debate's last challenger keeps pushing, and the warning that stopped Gargi comes true for him
381.tomorrow: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man?
381.howItsDone: The Vedic brahmodya, a formal contest of questions about Brahman, is the setting of this chapter; teachers of the Upanishads read Shakalya's end alongside Gargi's warning, and the closing tree verses are often recited on their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakalya's countdown: 3,306 gods, then 33, then 6, 3, 2, one and a half, and one. Your line was one. Truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. Day three hundred eighty-one.

The title of today's chapter sounds like a horror film, and the text tells it in a single plain sentence. But first, the build-up. After the countdown, Shakalya doesn't sit down. He keeps firing questions: the gods of each direction, what the heart rests on, what the self is founded on. Yajnavalkya answers each one. And somewhere in the middle he stops and asks Shakalya something. Shakalya, have these scholars made you their coal-tongs? Their tool for pulling hot coals out of the fire, so they don't burn their own hands?
screen: `HE DOESN'T SIT DOWN.` → `QUESTION AFTER QUESTION.` → `HAVE THEY MADE YOU THEIR COAL-TONGS?`

segments.voice: That line tells you what's going on. Shakalya isn't Gargi, chasing a question to its edge. The others have sent him in to do the burning work for them. And he keeps going. So at last Yajnavalkya turns the debate around. Now I ask you, he says, about the person taught in the Upanishads, the one who leads all these out, brings them back, and goes beyond them. If you can't tell me who he is, your head will fall off. Shakalya didn't know. And his head fell off. The text adds one more grim line: thieves carried off his bones, thinking they were something else. Then nothing more is said of him. How to hear this? The text doesn't explain. Some readers take it literally: in these Vedic debates on Brahman, the head was the stake, sworn to in advance. Many hear it as an image: his whole argument came apart; he lost face, the way we'd say it now. Either way, set it beside Gargi two days earlier. She got the very same warning, stopped, and came back later with better questions. Shakalya never stopped, and he was pushing as someone else's tool. Then the book's third chapter ends with a riddle. Yajnavalkya asks the room: a person is like a tree, hair for leaves, skin for bark. Cut a tree down, and it grows again from the root. From what root does a person grow, cut down by death? Nobody dares answer. The text answers instead: Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy.
screen: `SENT IN AS SOMEONE ELSE'S TOOL.` · `WHO IS THE PERSON OF THE UPANISHADS?` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW, AND HIS HEAD FELL.` · `FROM WHAT ROOT DOES A PERSON GROW?` · then, large: `DON'T ASK PAST THE LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the root. Sit, and breathe. Imagine yourself as a tree: hair like leaves, skin like bark, bones like the hard wood inside. Feel the weight of the body settle down into the seat, like roots into soil. Then ask the old riddle, without answering it: from what root do I grow? Let the question sit in the body, not the head. Breathe down into it. The bell holds the time.
Murdha. The head. In these debates, what you staked on your answer: lose the argument past a certain point, and the head was forfeit.
Your line: don't ask past the limit. Today, if you catch yourself asking a question to win rather than to know, stop, and ask a different one. Day three hundred eighty-one.

382.title: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man? sun → moon → fire → speech → self (4.3)
382.hook: a king asks what light a person has, and takes the lights away one at a time
382.tomorrow: dreaming — the self creates its own world
382.howItsDone: Hindus light lamps at dawn and dusk and at every festival, and the Brihadaranyaka's line that the self is a person's own light is often quoted by teachers when explaining the inner meaning of the lamp.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the debate ended: Shakalya pushed as someone else's tool, and lost his head. Your line was don't ask past the limit. Did you trade a question to win for one to know? Day three hundred eighty-two.

The power goes out at night. The streetlights die, the screens go black, your phone is at one percent and then it's gone. You can't see your own hand. And then, from the next room, someone calls your name. You get up and walk toward the voice. Something very like that moment is in the Brihadaranyaka, in a conversation between a king and a sage with no crowd and no cows. Just King Janaka, asking one question and taking the lights away one by one.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T SEE YOUR HAND.` → `YOU WALK TOWARD THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: The debate is over. In book four, Yajnavalkya visits the king again, quietly. Yajnavalkya, Janaka asks, what light does a person have? The sun, your majesty. By the light of the sun a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. True. But when the sun has set, what light does a person have? The moon. And when the sun has set and the moon has set? Fire. And when the sun has set, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out? Speech. That's why, when you can't even see your own hand, wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. True, Yajnavalkya. And when the sun has set, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, and speech has fallen silent, what light does a person have then? And Yajnavalkya says: atmaivasya jyotir bhavati. The self is their light. By the light of the self a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. Which is the self? The one made of knowing, among the senses, the light within the heart. Look at how carefully the king builds it. Each light is real, and each one can go out. The sun sets. The moon sets. Fire dies. Even voices go quiet. The question is what's left when all of them are gone. Sit in a dark room with your eyes open: nothing to look at, and still something knows it's dark. That knowing, the text says, is the light that was there under all the others.
screen: `THE SUN, THE MOON, THE FIRE.` · `SPEECH: WE WALK TOWARD A VOICE.` · `THE SELF IS THEIR LIGHT.` · `THE LIGHT WITHIN THE HEART.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes taking the lights away. Sit, and close your eyes. The sun has set: notice there's still something seeing the dark behind your eyelids. The moon has set; the fire's out: still knowing. Now let the voices go quiet, the ones outside and the one in your head. Rest in whatever is still aware. You don't need to name it. Just notice it's been on this whole time. The bell holds the time.
Jyoti. Light. In Janaka's question, what a person has when the sun, the moon, the fire and every voice are gone: the self is their light.
Your line: your own light. Tonight, when you turn off the last light, pause in the dark for one breath and notice what's still awake. Day three hundred eighty-two.

fork.reveal: wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. speech is a light too, until it falls silent and only the self is left.

original.note: Sanskrit jyotis: light. ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavati, the self is their light (4.3.6).

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle about the sun and the moon.
what it means: every outer light can go out; what is left, and was there all along, is the self.
what a scholar hears: kiṃjyotir ayaṃ puruṣa (4.3.2): the light-sequence leads to the self as 'the light within the heart' (hṛdy antarjyotiḥ, 4.3.7).

383.title: Dreaming — the self creates its own world (4.3)
383.hook: there are no roads or chariots in a dream, and yet you ride one: who built it?
383.tomorrow: deep sleep — the embrace of the beloved
383.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep, laid out in this part of the Brihadaranyaka and in the Mandukya Upanishad, to point to the self that is present in all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king took the lights away: sun, moon, fire, speech, until only one was left. The self is their light. Your line was your own light. What was still awake in the dark? Day three hundred eighty-three.

Last night, maybe, you were at a train station you've never seen. Someone who died years ago was there, talking normally. The house you grew up in had an extra room. And it all felt completely real until you woke. Nobody built that station. There's no train in your bedroom. So where did it come from, and what was lighting it, with your eyes closed in a dark room? Yajnavalkya keeps talking with King Janaka, and he turns to the place everyone visits every night.
screen: `A STATION YOU'VE NEVER SEEN.` → `NO TRAIN IN YOUR BEDROOM.` → `WHO BUILT IT?`

segments.voice: A person has two places, Yajnavalkya says: this world, and the other world. And there's a third, where the two meet: sleep, dreaming. Standing there, you can see both. When a person dreams, he takes the material of this whole world, tears it down himself, builds it up himself, and dreams by his own brightness, by his own light. There, the person is his own light. Then the passage that gives today its line. There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads. But he makes chariots, horses, roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, no delights. But he makes joys, pleasures, delights. There are no ponds, no lakes, no rivers. But he makes ponds, lakes, rivers. For he is the maker. Notice two things. First, the building material is borrowed: the station is made out of stations you've seen, the face out of faces you know. Nothing comes from nowhere. Second, the light. Yesterday, the self was the light left when the sun, the moon, fire and voice were gone. A dream is the proof. The room is dark, the eyes are shut, and still everything is lit. People see his playground, the text says, but nobody sees him. And a small, practical line, still good advice: don't wake a sleeping person suddenly, people say; it's hard to heal someone who doesn't find their way back. Later Hindu schools argued over who really does the building in a dream, the dreamer or God, and what dreams say about waking. The Upanishad leaves it here: the dreamer builds.
screen: `THE THIRD PLACE: WHERE TWO WORLDS MEET.` · `NO CHARIOTS THERE; HE MAKES THEM.` · `BORROWED MATERIAL, HIS OWN LIGHT.` · `THEY SEE HIS PLAYGROUND, NOT HIM.` · then, large: `THE DREAMER BUILDS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in the workshop. Sit, and close your eyes. Picture a place you love: a beach, a kitchen, a street. Build it slowly: the color of the walls, the sound, the smell. Notice you're making it, right now, out of things you've seen. Then notice it's lit, though your eyes are closed. Let the picture fade, and stay with that light, the one that was showing it to you. The bell holds the time.
Svayamjyoti. Self-luminous, lit by its own light. In a dream, Yajnavalkya says, the person is svayamjyoti: no sun, no lamp, and still everything shows.
Your line: the dreamer builds. Tomorrow morning, before you check your phone, remember one piece of your dream, and ask what light was showing it. Day three hundred eighty-three.

384.title: Deep sleep — the embrace of the beloved (4.3)
384.hook: the best night's sleep you ever had, with nothing in it, and something that still woke up rested
384.tomorrow: death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade
384.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use deep sleep, described here and in the Mandukya Upanishad, as an everyday clue to the self: something rests, and on waking, one knows one slept well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dreaming: no chariots, no roads, and the dreamer makes them, lit by his own light. Your line was the dreamer builds. Did you catch a piece of your dream this morning? Day three hundred eighty-four.

Some nights you sleep so deeply there's nothing to report. No dream, no time passing, no you. Then the alarm, and you sit up and say, I slept like a stone. It's the best sleep there is, and there was nobody there to enjoy it. Or was there? Who, exactly, slept well? Yesterday, Yajnavalkya took King Janaka into dreams. Today he goes one floor deeper, below the dreams, to the place you go every night and never remember.
screen: `NOTHING TO REPORT.` → `I SLEPT LIKE A STONE.` → `WHO SLEPT WELL?`

segments.voice: As a falcon or an eagle, Yajnavalkya says, tired from circling all day in the sky, folds its wings and heads home to its nest, so a person hurries to that state where, asleep, he wants nothing and sees no dream. Then the image this day is named for. As a man held by the one he loves knows nothing outside and nothing inside, so a person held by the knowing self knows nothing outside and nothing inside. That is the form, the text says, where every desire is met, because the self is the only desire, so there's no desire at all, and no sorrow. Then a list that sounds almost dangerous. There, a father is not a father, a mother not a mother. Worlds are not worlds, gods are not gods. A thief is not a thief. Untouched by good, untouched by evil, he has crossed every sorrow of the heart. Nothing you are in daylight follows you in. And yet the text insists this isn't a blank. When he doesn't see there, he is still seeing, for the seer's seeing is never lost. There's just no second thing to see. A few weeks ago, in the Chandogya, Indra turned deep sleep down. In deep sleep, he worried, you don't even know yourself; it's like being destroyed. Here Yajnavalkya calls it an embrace. Both are in the Upanishads, and Hindu teachers have held them together ever since. The Mandukya, which you met last year, names this state prajna, the third of the self's four quarters, and points past it to a fourth.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS.` · `HELD, KNOWING NOTHING OUTSIDE OR IN.` · `A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER.` · `INDRA'S DOUBT; YAJNAVALKYA'S EMBRACE.` · then, large: `NO INSIDE, NO OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes folding your wings. Sit, and breathe. Picture the falcon, tired, circling lower and lower. With each out-breath, fold something in: your plans for tonight, your name, your job, the role you play for other people. You're not trying to fall asleep. You're just letting the day's sky go. Rest in the nest, with nothing outside to watch and nothing inside to fix. The bell holds the time.
Deep sleep. No dream, no desire, no sorrow: a person held by prajna, the knowing self, with nothing outside and nothing inside. In the Mandukya, the third state.
Your line: no inside, no outside. Tonight, as you fall asleep, let the falcon fold its wings, and let the day's names go one by one. Day three hundred eighty-four.

385.title: Death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade (4.4)
385.hook: a small creature at the end of a blade of grass never lets go until it has hold of the next one
385.tomorrow: "as is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed"
385.howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, are performed by the family with fire and mantras, and the days that follow include offerings for the departed; passages like this one and Bhagavad Gita 2.22 are often read or recalled at the time of a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deep sleep: the falcon folding its wings, held by the knowing self, with no inside and no outside. Did the day's names go one by one as you fell asleep? Day three hundred eighty-five.

Crouch down in a garden and watch a caterpillar climb a blade of grass. When it reaches the tip, it doesn't fall off, and it doesn't jump. It stretches its front end out into the air, waving a little, until it touches the next blade. It grips. Only then does it let go of the old one and draw the rest of itself across. Yajnavalkya and King Janaka have walked through waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Now the king's teacher takes the last step, the one everyone takes, and he uses that caterpillar.
screen: `AT THE TIP OF A BLADE OF GRASS.` → `IT REACHES, AND GRIPS.` → `ONLY THEN DOES IT LET GO.`

segments.voice: First he describes the dying, gently and closely. The person grows weak and seems confused. The senses gather around the self, the way a king's officers gather when he's about to travel. The self draws all its powers in and goes down into the heart. People around the bed say: he doesn't see now, he doesn't hear now. He's becoming one. Then the tip of the heart lights up, and by that light the self leaves, and the breath and the senses follow. And what goes with it? What it knew, and what it did, and what it had lived. Then the picture. As a caterpillar, coming to the end of a blade of grass, reaches out to another and draws itself across, so the self, having laid down this body and let go of not-knowing, reaches out to another support and draws itself across. And one more: as a goldsmith takes a piece of gold and hammers it into another shape, newer and more beautiful, so the self makes itself another form. Notice what these pictures say. There's no gap in the caterpillar's crossing: it doesn't let go into nothing. And the gold is the same gold. You met Krishna's picture in the Gita last year, old clothes laid aside for new ones; it belongs to the same family. Look back at this week. Gargi's two arrows. The gods counted down to one. Shakalya's head. The light of the self. The dreamer building. Deep sleep's embrace. And today, the leaf.
screen: `THE SENSES GATHER; THE HEART LIGHTS UP.` · `WHAT IT KNEW, DID, AND LIVED GOES WITH IT.` · `THE CATERPILLAR REACHES THE NEXT BLADE.` · `THE GOLDSMITH'S GOLD, NEWLY SHAPED.` · then, large: `THE LEAF.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of reaching and letting go. Sit, and breathe. At the very end of each out-breath, notice the tiny reach toward the next breath, before the old one is quite finished. Then let the old breath go. Don't hurry it. If thoughts about death come, someone you've lost, or your own, let them be here too, and keep breathing through them, one blade to the next. The bell holds the time.
Death, as the Brihadaranyaka pictures it: a caterpillar at the tip of a blade of grass, reaching for the next before it lets go.
Your line: the leaf. Today, when you finish something, notice whether you've already reached for the next thing before you let go. Day three hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 385 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "AS IS HIS DESIRE, SO IS HIS WILL."`

fork.setup: you're a caterpillar at the very tip of a blade of grass. what do you do?
options: reach out, grip the next blade, then draw yourself across.
fork.reveal: it reaches, grips, and only then lets go. so, the text says, the self lays down this body and draws itself across to another support.

original.note: Sanskrit tṛṇa (grass) + jalāyukā: a creature that moves blade to blade; translators say caterpillar or leech.

trapdoor: what you thought: death is a fall into nothing.
what it means: in this picture, the self reaches the next support before it lets go, carrying what it knew and did.
what a scholar hears: 4.4.3's tṛṇajalāyukā is rendered caterpillar or leech; 4.4.4's goldsmith and Gita 2.22's clothes are kindred images of rebirth.
